description_full: Carlisle Companies Incorporated operates as a manufacturer and supplier of building envelope products and solutions in the United States, Europe, North America, and internationally. It operates through two segments, Carlisle Construction Materials (CCM) and Carlisle Weatherproofing Technologies (CWT). The CCM segment offers single-ply roofing solutions, including ethylene propylene diene monomer, thermoplastic polyolefin, polyvinyl chloride membrane, polyiso insulation, and engineered metal roofing and wall panel systems for commercial and residential buildings. Its CWT segment provides waterproofing and moisture protection products; protective roofing underlayment; fully integrated liquid and sheet applied air/vapor barriers; sealants/primers and flashing systems; roof coatings and mastics; spray polyurethane foam and coating systems for a range of thermal protection applications and other premium polyurethane products; block-molded expanded polystyrene insulation; engineered products for HVAC applications; and products for a variety of industrial and surfacing applications. The company sells its products under the Carlisle SynTec, Versico, WeatherBond, Hunter Panels, Resitrix, and Hertalan brands. The company was founded in 1917 and is headquartered in Scottsdale, Arizona.

financial_summary: Carlisle Companies Incorporated is a large-cap industrials business with a $15.3B market cap on $5.0B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -9% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 19% against a 8% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 27%.

The business throws off $971M in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.49× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.5× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 13× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 9.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
